title: Probing Strain, Stacking, and Switching of van der Walls Materials using 4D-STEM
content: Van der Waals (vdW) materials exhibit highly versatile properties, making them promising candidates for future applications in electronics, optoelectronics, and quantum computing. The local structure, including strain, stacking order, and interlayer sliding, plays a critical role in dictating these properties by influencing domain structure, charge transport, and even topological states. Recent advances in four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) have significantly improved our ability to visualize and quantify local structural variations at the atomic scale[1] . By capturing a diffraction pattern at each probe position, 4D-STEM allows for detailed strain mapping[2-4] , orientation analysis[5,6] , and structural characterization with deep sub-angstrom resolution[7-9] . This technique provides unprecedented insights into nanoscale heterogeneities, enabling researchers to unravel complex strain fields, domain structures, and stacking configurations in vdW materials with high precision. These capabilities not only deepen our understanding of fundamental physical phenomena but also facilitate the rational design and engineering of vdW materials for advanced technological applications.
